messages.subject: Fwd: Efficiently draw Monte Carlo Samples from Posterior Predictive
parts:
Hi Stanners,  I'm using vb() in rstan to estimate a GP model similar to that described in the manual for NT = 2500 observations with P = 2 predictors under varying length scales in a squared exponential covariance formula.   The stan script, below, builds an MCMC model for the parameters of the covariance formula.  My interest is to extract the latent (de-noised) function, which i sample from the posterior predictive distribution in the generated quantities block.  The advi estimate is returned in about 2 hours, but it has not yet completed generating 1000 samples after a day.   The long time period is not due to returning samples of the parameters (since I have separately run that and validated such) but due to the monte carlo draws from the posterior predictive for the latent function.  Since the generated quantities block draws monte carlo samples, only, i'm assuming there are no gradients to compute.   I'd appreciate any tips on how I might re-configure the script in the generated quantities block to speed up the generated monte carlo samples.   

/*
  y[c] ~ N_{T}(u[c], sigma_y[c]),  where c = 1,..,NT are domain-time case. sigma_y[c] are known
  // squared exponential covariance function for NT x NT covariance matrix, Sigma
  Sigma[i,j] = 1/eta * sum_{c=1}^{NT}sum_{c'=1}^{NT}
                            sum_{p=1}^{P} exp(-1/rho[p](x[c,p] - x[c',p])^{2})
  u[1] ,..., u[NT] ~ * N_{NT}(0, Sigma),
  eta     ~ Gamma(1,1) - precision parameter of squared exponential covariance function 
  rho[k]  ~ Gamma(1,1) - predictor indexed length-scale parameters
  
  We may marginalize over the u to achieve
  y[c] ~ N_{T}(0, Sigma + diag(sigma2_y))
  
  Marginalizing over u adds the known response variances, sigma2_y, to the diagonals
  which stabilizes the cholesky computation for Sigma (which is very high-dimensional).
  We use the properties of the Gaussian wrapper in which the nonparametric GP is parameterized
  to draw u as a post-processing step using sampled values of c(rho,eta)

*/

data{
  int<lower=1> NT; // number of domain-months
  int<lower=1> P; // number of predictors
  vector[NT] y; // vectorized response variable, with T faster than N
  matrix[NT,P] x; // Set of NT, 1 x P predictors
  vector<lower=0>[NT] sigma2_y; // known domain variances
  real<lower=0> jitter; // stabilizing constant to add to diagonals of GP cov, Sigma */
} /* end data block */
  

transformed data{
  vector[NT] zros_NT;
  zros_NT <- rep_vector(0,NT); /* vector of zeros for sampling Tx1 fixed effects, beta */
} /* end transformed data block */

parameters{
  // parameters for squared exponential covariance function
  real<lower=0> eta; /* rational quadratic precision parameter */
  real<lower=0> rho[P]; /* length-scale parameters, indexed by predictor, x[,p] */
} /* end parameters block */

transformed parameters{
  matrix[NT,NT] Sigma; /* GP covariance matrix for NT x 1, u */
  matrix[NT,NT] K; /* GP covariance matrix for u */
  matrix[NT,NT] L; /* cholesky_decompose(Sigma) */
  
  { /* local block */
    real covformula_ijp;
    real s_ij;
     // off-diagonal
    for( i in 1:(NT-1) )
    {
      for( j in (i+1):NT )
      {
        s_ij <- 0;
        for( p in 1:P )
        {
          covformula_ijp      <- inv(rho[p])* pow(x[i,p] - x[j,p],2);
          s_ij                <- s_ij + covformula_ijp ;
        }/* end loop p over dimensions of x to fill cells of Sigma */
        s_ij       <-  exp( -s_ij ) ;
        s_ij       <-  inv(eta) * s_ij;
        K[i,j]     <- s_ij;
        K[j,i]     <- s_ij;
      } /* end loop j over columns to fill upper triangular cells of Sigma */
    } /* end loop i over rows to fill upper triangular cells of Sigma */
    
    // diagonal
    for( k in 1:NT )
    {
      for( p in 1:P )
      {
        K[k,k]     <- inv(eta) + jitter;
      } /* end loop p over dimensions of x to fill cells of Sigma */
    } /* end loop k over diagonal entries of Sigma */
  } /* end local block for building Sigma */
  
  /* add model noise on the diagonal to achieve the marginal distribution */
  /* of y */
  Sigma     <- K + diag_matrix( sigma2_y );
  L         <- cholesky_decompose( Sigma );
  
} /* end transformed parameters block */


model{
  
  // priors for mean and covariance cluster location 
  eta       ~ gamma( 1.0, 1.0 );
  rho       ~ gamma( 1.0, 1.0 );
  
   
  // observed response likelihood
  y         ~ multi_normal_cholesky(zros_NT,L);
  
  
  
} /* end model{} block */

generated quantities{
  matrix[NT,NT] K_transpose_div_Sigma; /* K'Sigma^-1 */
  matrix[NT,NT] Tau; /* posterior predictive covariance matrix for u */
  matrix[NT,NT] L_u;
  vector[NT] mu_u; /* predictive mean of NT x 1, u */
  vector[NT] u; /* GP function drawn from posterior predictive */
  /* compute MSE for fit evaluation */
  real<lower=0> TSE;
  real<lower=0> MSE;
  /* posterior predictive quantities */
  K_transpose_div_Sigma  <- K' / Sigma;
  mu_u                   <- K_transpose_div_Sigma * y;
  Tau                    <- K - K_transpose_div_Sigma * K;
  L_u                    <- cholesky_decompose( Tau );
  u   <- multi_normal_cholesky_rng(mu_u,L_u);
  TSE <- squared_distance(u,y);
  MSE <- TSE/(NT);
  
  
} /* end generated quantities block */

I also used a variation on the above script for generated quantities that leverages the cholesky decomposition of Sigma that is already computed, but there was no speed improvement.

generated quantities{
  matrix[NT,NT] div_L_K; /* L^-1 * K */
  matrix[NT,NT] Tau; /* posterior predictive covariance matrix for u */
  matrix[NT,NT] L_u; /* cholesky of Tau */
  vector[NT] mu_u; /* predictive mean of NT x 1, u */
  vector[NT] u; /* GP function drawn from posterior predictive */
  /* compute MSE for fit evaluation */
  real<lower=0> TSE;
  real<lower=0> MSE;
  /* posterior predictive quantities */
  div_L_K                <- mdivide_left_tri_low(L,K);
  mu_u                   <- div_L_K' * mdivide_left_tri_low(L,y);
  Tau                    <- K - div_L_K' * div_L_K;
  // for( i in 1:(NT-1))
  // {
  //   for( j in (i+1):NT)
  //   {
  //     Tau[i,j]  <- Tau[j,i];
  //   }
  // }
  L_u <- cholesky_decompose(Tau);
  u   <- multi_normal_cholesky_rng(mu_u,L_u);
  TSE <- squared_distance(u,y);
  MSE <- TSE/(NT);
  
  
} /* end generated quantities block */

Thanks very much your help and comments.

Terrance

Thank you, Terrance Savitsky

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Efficiently draw Monte Carlo Samples from Posterior Predictive [ADVI]
parts:
You'll need someone who knows the ADVI code and linear algebra
better than me to help at a deeper level.

In NUTS/HMC, the generated quantities are run once per iteration,
not at the end. So I don't know how you get the ADVI estimate in
2 hours then hang after that. But then I don't know how ADVI is
working w.r.t. generated quantities.

Might you be running into problems with memory swapping or
file I/O with the size? And do you really need 1000 draws?

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Efficiently draw Monte Carlo Samples from Posterior Predictive [ADVI]
parts:
Hi Bob, I appreciate your response.   The linear algebra is pretty efficient; in fact, I was going to suggest it for the manual since the efficient (NUTS) sampling procedure is to sample using the cholesky.   So i just use that and the nice functions mdivide_left_tri_low().  But i digress.  I think maybe ADVI also generates quantities once per iteration.   The cholesky of the high-dimensional covariance matrix is already computed for sampling, so it would seem to be relatively quick to generate a monte carlo draw.    If this is the case, I don't know why the model converges after 2 hours and then hangs indefinitely for generating samples.   To your point about hitting memory limits, I've reduced the number of samples to 200, but still the same problem.  I'll try 100, next.   Lastly, one subtle point that i would really appreciate to have clarified is whether - under ADVI and also NUTS - there is any benefit or cost taking the cholesky of a covariance matrix used to generate a quantity from some distribution.  Unlike under sampling, I would think it doesn't matter for generated quantities.

Thank you,

Terrance.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Efficiently draw Monte Carlo Samples from Posterior Predictive [ADVI]
parts:
I don't think it should be taking that long so there might be something fishy going on. Either way I don't think you need the cholesky parameterization in generated quantities. I think you'd only really need it if you didn't need to additionally do the decomposition (you already had the cholesky factor). I'm not sure if that will solve the problem though. What you describe seems excessive regardless.

Jonah

parts:
If you can do a Cholesky factorization once, it's much
better than doing it N times. But if you only do it once,
then no worries.

But I just realized the reason ADVI may be hanging after
getting the posterior mean is that I think it then does
multivariate normal draws around the variational approximation
and converts back to the constrained space. That's probably
where the time's going, not into generated quantities.

You could always try running iterations in Stan with
fixed parameters just to run generated quantities (then you
have to feed it the parameter values as inits or just
use the random inits).

- Bob

The linear algebra is pretty efficient; in fact, I was going to suggest it for the manual since the efficient (NUTS) sampling procedure is to sample using the cholesky. So i just use that and the nice functions mdivide_left_tri_low(). But i digress. I think maybe ADVI also generates quantities once per iteration. The cholesky of the high-dimensional covariance matrix is already computed for sampling, so it would seem to be relatively quick to generate a monte carlo draw. If this is the case, I don't know why the model converges after 2 hours and then hangs indefinitely for generating samples. To your point about hitting memory limits, I've reduced the number of samples to 200, but still the same problem. I'll try 100, next. Lastly, one subtle point that i would really appreciate to have clarified is whether - under ADVI and also NUTS - there is any benefit or cost taking the cholesky of a covariance matrix used to generate a quantity from some distribution. messages.author: 33d5534e21fbbe0f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Efficiently draw Monte Carlo Samples from Posterior Predictive [ADVI]
parts:
Hi Bob and Jonah,  I write to report back on a partial resolution for drawing samples of a GP latent function from the posterior predictive when estimating using ADVI.   I was reading Bob's JSS paper and a comment there prompted the realization that I was hitting a memory ceiling because I declared high dimensional covariance objects as global in the generated quantities block.  The revised script, below, creates a local block within generated quantities where these covariance objects are now declared locally.   That step eliminated the memory ceiling issue on my machine, though there is a huge amount of temporary memory cache that isn't released when i manually gc() in R, which will be an issue for users to whom I will transfer this model.  It seems odd because the big jump in memory usage occurs after estimation - when generating  samples - but the large objects are all declared as local.   

Anyway, drawing the samples for the latent GP function does take longer than for other models - around an hour - for 100 samples which is certainly acceptable.  So the whole model, below, successfully converges and produces 100 samples in about 3.25 hours.   The estimates are quite good (as verified on synthetic data). While I've experienced some local optima for more heavily parameterized models using ADVI, I find with a little fiddling that I always get high quality estimates.  I use ADVI because I'm trying to fit usefully rich and flexible Bayesian approaches in a production process for economic statistics that is both very orchestrated and time-constrained.  They won't wait a week or two for an MCMC scheme to complete.   I often write a sampling algorithm in C++, but it is used as a black box by the production folks - so they are a little suspicious of black boxes.  Although they don't understand the estimation algorithms used in Stan, they like the expressive syntax in .stan files for model exposition (which is why I add a lot of comments).   They also like the ability to relatively easily change prior formulations.   Stan is helping to reduce the resistance to the practical use of bayesian models.  


Thanks for your help,

Terrance

/*
  y[c] ~ N_{T}(u[c], sigma_y[c]),  where c = 1,..,NT are domain-time case. sigma_y[c] are known
  // squared exponential covariance function for NT x NT covariance matrix, Sigma
  Sigma[i,j] = 1/eta * sum_{c=1}^{NT}sum_{c'=1}^{NT}
                            sum_{p=1}^{P} exp(-1/rho[p](x[c,p] - x[c',p])^{2})
  u[1] ,..., u[NT] ~ * N_{NT}(0, Sigma),
  eta     ~ Gamma(1,1) - precision parameter of squared exponential covariance function 
  rho[k]  ~ Gamma(1,1) - predictor indexed length-scale parameters
  
  We may marginalize over the u to achieve
  y[c] ~ N_{T}(0, Sigma + diag(sigma2_y))
  
  Marginalizing over u adds the known response variances, sigma2_y, to the diagonals
  which stabilizes the cholesky computation for Sigma (which is very high-dimensional).
  We use the properties of the Gaussian wrapper in which the nonparametric GP is parameterized
  to draw u as a post-processing step using sampled values of c(rho,eta)

*/

data{
  int<lower=1> NT; // number of domain-months
  int<lower=1> P; // number of predictors
  vector[NT] y; // vectorized response variable, with T faster than N
  matrix[NT,P] x; // Set of NT, 1 x P predictors
  vector<lower=0>[NT] sigma2_y; // known domain variances
  real<lower=0> jitter; // stabilizing constant to add to diagonals of GP cov, Sigma */
} /* end data block */
  

transformed data{
  vector[NT] zros_NT;
  zros_NT <- rep_vector(0,NT); /* vector of zeros for sampling Tx1 fixed effects, beta */
} /* end transformed data block */

parameters{
  // parameters for squared exponential covariance function
  real<lower=0> eta; /* rational quadratic precision parameter */
  real<lower=0> rho[P]; /* length-scale parameters, indexed by predictor, x[,p] */
} /* end parameters block */

transformed parameters{
  matrix[NT,NT] Sigma; /* GP covariance matrix for NT x 1, u */
  matrix[NT,NT] K; /* GP covariance matrix for u */
  matrix[NT,NT] L; /* cholesky_decompose(Sigma) */
  
  { /* local block */
    real covformula_ijp;
    real s_ij;
     // off-diagonal
    for( i in 1:(NT-1) )
    {
      for( j in (i+1):NT )
      {
        s_ij <- 0;
        for( p in 1:P )
        {
          covformula_ijp      <- inv(rho[p])* pow(x[i,p] - x[j,p],2);
          s_ij                <- s_ij + covformula_ijp ;
        }/* end loop p over dimensions of x to fill cells of Sigma */
        s_ij       <-  exp( -s_ij ) ;
        s_ij       <-  inv(eta) * s_ij;
        K[i,j]     <- s_ij;
        K[j,i]     <- s_ij;
      } /* end loop j over columns to fill upper triangular cells of Sigma */
    } /* end loop i over rows to fill upper triangular cells of Sigma */
    
    // diagonal
    for( k in 1:NT )
    {
      for( p in 1:P )
      {
        K[k,k]     <- inv(eta) + jitter;
      } /* end loop p over dimensions of x to fill cells of Sigma */
    } /* end loop k over diagonal entries of Sigma */
  } /* end local block for building Sigma */
  
  /* add model noise on the diagonal to achieve the marginal distribution */
  /* of y */
  Sigma     <- K + diag_matrix( sigma2_y );
  L         <- cholesky_decompose( Sigma );
  
} /* end transformed parameters block */


model{
  
  // priors for mean and covariance cluster location 
  eta       ~ gamma( 1.0, 1.0 );
  rho       ~ gamma( 1.0, 1.0 );
  
   
  // observed response likelihood
  y         ~ multi_normal_cholesky(zros_NT,L);
  
  
  
} /* end model{} block */

generated quantities{

vector[NT] u; /* GP function drawn from posterior predictive */
  /* compute MSE for fit evaluation */
  real<lower=0> TSE;
  real<lower=0> MSE;
  /* posterior predictive quantities */
{ /* environment to declar local variables */

matrix[NT,NT] div_L_K; /* L^-1 * K */
    matrix[NT,NT] Tau; /* posterior predictive covariance matrix for u */
    matrix[NT,NT] L_u; /* cholesky of Tau */
    vector[NT] mu_u; /* predictive mean of NT x 1, u */
div_L_K                <- mdivide_left_tri_low(L,K);

mu_u                   <- div_L_K' * mdivide_left_tri_low(L,y);
    Tau                    <- K - div_L_K' * div_L_K;
L_u <- cholesky_decompose(Tau);

u   <- multi_normal_cholesky_rng(mu_u,L_u);
    TSE <- squared_distance(u,y);
    MSE <- TSE/(NT);
} /* end local variable block */
} /* end generated quantities block */

> >   rho       ~ gamma( 1.0, 1.0 );
> >
> >
> >   // observed response likelihood
> >   y         ~ multi_normal_cholesky(zros_NT,L);

> >
> >
> > } /* end model{} block */

> >   vector[NT] mu_u; /* predictive mean of NT x 1, u */
> >   vector[NT] u; /* GP function drawn from posterior predictive */
> >   /* compute MSE for fit evaluation */
> >   real<lower=0> TSE;

> >   /* posterior predictive quantities */
> >   K_transpose_div_Sigma  <- K' / Sigma;
> >   mu_u                   <- K_transpose_div_Sigma * y;
